etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English convenient, from Latin conveniens (“fit, suitable, convenient”), present participle of convenire (“to come together, suit”); see convene and compare covenant.

definitions.definition: Serving to reduce a difficulty, or accessible with minimum difficulty; expedient.
Suspicious due to suiting someone's purposes very well.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs 30:8:
quote.text: Feed me with food convenient for me.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Ephesians 5:4:
quote.text: Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient.

quote.citation: 1640, Edward Reynolds, A treatise of the passions and faculties of the soule of man:
quote.text: […]  continual drinking is most convenient to the distemper of an hydropick body, though most disconvenient to its present welfare.
